archetype.name: Dual-Threat (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A 12th-year former No. 2 pick who now backs up Jayden Daniels and wins in relief with a shotgun quick game, accurate short throws and the occasional designed run, rather than by pushing the ball downfield.

report.headline: Efficient in relief, but a 51-attempt sample built on catch-up throws and luck.
report.take:
Mariota is Washington's QB2 and has been all season. Jayden Daniels started every game the dossier lists except Week 4, and Mariota's three appearances add up to 51 attempts: a relief half at Dallas, the full Seattle win, and a Week 4 start that lasted 16% of the snaps. His rate stats look strong. He is 10th in EPA per dropback at 0.168 and 10th in CPOE at 3.89, against a league average of -0.027 EPA. He has thrown no interceptions, and his 7.8% TD rate ranks 3rd. Fifty-one attempts can't carry that much weight, though, and the shape of the production matters more than the totals.

The real part is the short game. On throws of 0-9 air yards he has 30 attempts at 0.284 EPA, a 76.7% completion rate and 8.9 CPOE. That fits who he has been: his 2025 CPOE was 3.2, and he has posted a positive CPOE in most of his seasons. Terry McLaurin (0.348 EPA per target on 13 targets) is where the efficiency comes from. Mariota is also throwing less aggressively than last year (14.89% tight-window throws vs 19.8%), which fits a backup taking what the defense gives.

What the numbers hide is context and luck. His 12 dropbacks while trailing by 9 or more produced 0.494 EPA, much of it during the Dallas relief outing, while his 42 plays within one score came in at -0.007, roughly league-average football. He converted only 26.7% of his third downs. Three of his four TDs came on four red-zone attempts. His deep ball is 2-of-8 and carries no value overall, even though both completions were touchdowns. The pressure numbers are the clearest warning. He was pressured on 38.9% of dropbacks, the worst rate among 45 qualifiers, yet took sacks on only 14.3% of those pressures, the best mark. For his whole career he has sat near the bottom of the league in that stat (0.314 last year, 0.365 to 0.417 earlier). That is a small-sample streak, not a new skill.

Going forward he is insurance. If Daniels misses time, expect a competent, mostly short-area passer with real running ability, closer to his 2025 self (7.47 YPA, some interceptions) than to the turnover-free, TD-heavy line he has now.

strengths.title: Accurate, efficient short passing
strengths.body: His 30 short attempts carry 0.284 EPA and 8.9 CPOE, which accounts for most of his value. Accuracy over expectation has been a steady trait: his 2025 CPOE was 3.2 and ranked 13th. This is the part of his profile most likely to hold up if he plays more.

strengths.title: Legs still add value
strengths.body: Two designed runs averaged 22 yards each, and his rushing rate of 16.3 yards a game ranks 19th despite limited snaps. He has ranked in the top 13 in QB rushing yards in every full season the dossier lists. That gives a defense a real extra problem even at 33.

strengths.title: Clean with the football
strengths.body: No interceptions, no lost fumbles and no turnover-worthy plays on the season. The short, safe throw selection drives this, so it is partly a product of the role. Last year he threw 0.78 picks a game, so expect some interceptions with more volume.

concerns.title: Sack avoidance is borrowed luck
concerns.body: He faced pressure more often than any qualifier, yet turned the fewest pressures into sacks. Every season with charting data has put him near the bottom in pressure-to-sack rate. With Laremy Tunsil on IR and not expected back this regular season, the protection won't improve, and the sacks should return.

concerns.title: Efficiency leans on catch-up mode
concerns.body: His trailing-by-9+ plays posted 0.494 EPA. His one-score plays sat at -0.007 and produced all three sacks. Third downs (26.7% converted, -0.231 EPA) are where competitive defenses held him in check. That is the version a full-time start would bring.

concerns.title: TD rate won't hold
concerns.body: A 7.8% TD rate built on three red-zone scores from four attempts and two deep completions that both went for touchdowns is a coin-flip streak. His career TD rates have sat in normal ranges, and he is at 25% completions on deep throws.

trend.note: His usage has swung from a relief half in Dallas (5.0 EPA) to the full Seattle win (3 TDs, 3.9 EPA) to a Week 4 start that lasted 16% of the snaps. He hasn't thrown a pass since, as Daniels has started every game after that.

nextGame.headline: Backup again; Arizona's broken pass defense matters only if he plays.
nextGame.body:
On paper this is the best passing matchup in the league. Arizona ranks last in pass EPA allowed (0.279), 31st against short throws (0.213), where Mariota does his best work, and last in both fantasy points and TDs allowed to quarterbacks. Its run defense is respectable (10th), which tilts things further toward the pass. But Mariota is listed as QB2, and nothing in the dossier puts Daniels on the injury report, so the base case is that he holds a clipboard.

The opening for snaps is game script. Arizona will be without its quarterback Carson Beck (back) and guard Jon Gaines II. That helps explain why Washington is a 7.5-point road favorite with a -399 moneyline. A comfortable lead could mean late relief work, as in Dallas, but that is a few handoffs and safe throws, not a stat line. The Kaliakmanis inactive note only confirms the depth chart: Mariota is the active backup.

keyMatchups.title: Short game vs. soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Arizona gives up 0.213 EPA on short passes. That plays straight into Mariota's 0-9 yard accuracy, should he play meaningful snaps. Any drives he runs would likely be efficient even without big plays.

keyMatchups.title: McLaurin against Arizona's WR1 coverage
keyMatchups.body: Arizona has held top receivers under their averages (5th by points over average) while allowing 0.51 EPA per target to them. That mixed record makes McLaurin, Mariota's most productive target, a real but not certain outlet.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script, garbage snaps
keyMatchups.body: With Beck out and Washington a heavy favorite, a lopsided fourth quarter is plausible. That is the most likely way Mariota sees the field, and it would bring run-heavy, low-volume work.

nextGame.watch: Daniels' status on the final injury report: Mariota's outlook depends entirely on whether he plays.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as Daniels is healthy, Mariota's expected output is close to zero. What matters is the version Washington would get in a spot start. The short accuracy and the rushing are real and long-standing. The zero interceptions, the 7.8% TD rate and the near-absence of sacks under heavy pressure are not, and his career says all three revert. A realistic starter's line looks like his 2025 self: about 180 to 230 passing yards, one to two TDs, an interception roughly every other game, and 15 to 35 rushing yards.

The environment around him is middling: a 19th-ranked offense, a pass rate close to neutral, and no Tunsil returning to help a line that let him be pressured on nearly four in ten dropbacks. He is a capable short-term bridge, not someone who raises the offense's ceiling. The projections below are per game he starts.
swingFactors: Whether sacks under pressure return to his career norm

confidence.note: 51 attempts in a backup role with one full game; usage depends on another QB's availability.
